strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the datamodels framework to robot imitation learning, addressing the core obstacle (expensive/dangerous rollouts) via a differentiable proxy metric (validation BC loss) that is empirically shown to correlate well with true rollout success (Fig. 2).

Two complementary datamodel estimators (regression and metagradient-based) are proposed, enabling both a more accurate but expensive method and a scalable method usable with large transformer/diffusion policies like Octo.

Extensive empirical validation across 60+ tasks spanning three regimes of increasing difficulty: MetaWorld (MLP policies, state input), LIBERO (Octo, RGB input), and real-world OXE experiments across multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid) including cross-embodiment and multi-task settings.

Consistent and often large improvements over multiple strong, relevant heuristic baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR/SR), with particularly compelling results in the more heterogeneous/OOD real-world OXE setting.

Thoughtful practical adaptations for robotics (trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce noise, mixing target data during datamodel estimation to reduce distribution shift) that are ablated/justified rather than just asserted.

Good qualitative analysis of selected data (Figures 5-8) that provides interpretability into why DataMIL outperforms heuristics (e.g., correctly filtering suboptimal actions, selecting diverse yet relevant sources across embodiments).
Reasonably transparent limitations section and honest discussion of discrepancies with prior reported STRAP numbers, aiding reproducibility trust.
weaknesses: Real-world OXE evaluations are conducted with a single random seed and relatively small numbers of rollouts per task (as few as 10-40), which is a significant concern for the statistical reliability of the main real-world claims, especially given inherent variance in physical robot experiments.

Computational cost of DataMIL remains substantial even with the metagradient estimator (several times the cost of standard training per the Limitations section), and the paper does not provide a thorough head-to-head wall-clock/cost comparison against the (typically cheap) similarity-based baselines in the main text.

Key hyperparameters (selection ratio x%, clustering granularity, α=0.5 co-training ratio) appear to be tuned somewhat ad hoc/per-dataset without a principled selection procedure or sensitivity analysis, which the authors acknowledge but do not fully address.

Missing comparisons to some data-curation baselines discussed in Related Work that are also performance/end-to-end aware (e.g., Re-Mix, mutual-information-based curation, online-experience curation), which could better contextualize DataMIL's advantage over methods that aren't purely similarity-heuristic based.

The MetaWorld prior dataset construction (mixing scripted-expert and SAC-replay-buffer data) and the specific noise/quality characteristics of this synthetic setup may not fully represent realistic large-scale heterogeneous datasets, somewhat limiting generalizability of the MetaWorld results.

Discrepancy with STRAP's originally reported LIBERO numbers, while explained, still leaves some ambiguity about how much of DataMIL's advantage stems from evaluation protocol/policy architecture choices versus the selection method itself.

strengths: Novel and timely application of the datamodels framework to robot imitation learning, addressing the genuine challenge that policy rollouts are too expensive to directly estimate data influence.

The proposed differentiable proxy metric (loss on held-out target demonstrations) as a substitute for rollout-based success rate is a sensible and practically important contribution, and the paper empirically validates (on one task) that it correlates reasonably well with the true objective while enabling much cheaper metagradient-based estimation.

Broad experimental scope spanning simulated benchmarks (MetaWorld, LIBERO) and real-world manipulation with heterogeneous OXE data across multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid), which is relatively rare and valuable in this line of work.

Thoughtful adaptations to make datamodels tractable for robotics: trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce variance, and mixing a fraction of target data into prior data during estimation to counter distribution shift.

Interesting qualitative analyses (Figures 5-8) showing what data DataMIL selects versus heuristic baselines, offering some interpretability and insight into failure modes of similarity-based retrieval methods.
Comparisons against a reasonably comprehensive set of relevant heuristic baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR, SR) across all experimental settings.
weaknesses: All real-world (OXE) evaluations were run with a single random seed, which is a serious concern given that the real-world results are presented as the paper's most notable contribution ("most notably showing successful data selection from OXE"); without repeated trials, the reported gains (e.g., Franka-Pouch 70.6 vs 41.2 for BR) cannot be judged for statistical reliability, especially given typical variance in real robot rollouts.

The validation that the proxy metric correlates with true rollout success (Figure 2) is performed on only a single MetaWorld task (pick-place-wall), which is a weak empirical basis for a central claim that underlies the entire method's applicability to real-world/rollout-free settings.

Per-task LIBERO results (Table 3) show substantial overlap in confidence intervals between DataMIL and the strongest baselines (e.g., Soup-Sauce, Stove-Moka, Bowl-Cabinet, Mug-Mug, Mug-Pudding, Moka-Moka), and DataMIL is not the best performer on several individual tasks, undermining the claim of "consistent gains... over multiple baselines."

The method still requires several full/partial policy trainings and gradient computations to estimate datamodels—the paper's own limitations section admits this cost is "several times" that of training on all data, which is in tension with the motivation of avoiding expensive procedures, and no wall-clock/compute comparison against baselines is given to substantiate practicality claims.

Discrepancy with the originally reported STRAP numbers is explained post-hoc (evaluation protocol and policy architecture differences) but raises concerns about whether all baselines were tuned/implemented with equal care, particularly since baseline hyperparameters (e.g., horizon length, selection ratio) appear to have been selected via the authors' own preliminary experiments rather than a principled or jointly-optimized procedure.

Key design choices (clustering granularity, selection percentage x%, co-training ratio α=0.5, up-weighting factors for "pre-grasp" states) are set largely by trial-and-error per dataset, which the paper candidly lists as a limitation, but this undercuts the generality and plug-and-play usability of the proposed framework.

The metagradient-based estimator itself is adopted wholesale from prior work (Engstrom et al., Ilyas & Engstrom) rather than developed in this paper; the core technical novelty is largely confined to the proxy-metric substitution and robotics-specific engineering choices (clustering, distribution-shift mitigation), which are reasonable but incremental rather than fundamentally new methodological contributions.

Real-world target tasks are still relatively narrow in scope (single-task or small multitask settings with limited demonstrations/evaluations, e.g., 10-39 rollouts per task), which the authors acknowledge limits conclusions about large-scale data curation scenarios where curation is argued to matter most.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the datamodels framework to robot imitation learning, addressing the key obstacle (need for real rollouts) via a differentiable proxy metric based on held-out validation loss, which is carefully validated empirically against true rollout success (Fig. 2).

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO tasks with a large transformer/diffusion policy (Octo), and real-world experiments on OXE spanning multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid) and both single- and multi-task settings.

Strong and consistent improvements over multiple relevant heuristic baselines (BR, Flow, STRAP, AR, SR) across nearly all settings, including especially compelling real-world results where DataMIL selects useful cross-embodiment data even for embodiments entirely absent from the prior dataset (Tiago-Sink).

Thoughtful engineering adaptations to make datamodels tractable/robust for robotics: cluster-level influence estimation (with data-size-dependent granularity), and explicit handling of distribution shift for heterogeneous real-world datasets.

Good qualitative analysis (Section 5.2 and Appendix A) of what data is selected, offering intuition for why DataMIL outperforms heuristics (e.g., selecting broader, more general data; distinguishing helpful vs. harmful near-identical states).
Transparent limitations section and candid discussion of discrepancies with prior reported STRAP numbers, indicating scientific care.
Detailed appendix with formal problem statement, estimator derivations, baseline implementation details, and per-task experimental configurations, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely an adaptation/combination of existing techniques (datamodels, metagradients, influence functions) to a new domain rather than a fundamentally new estimation method; novelty is more in engineering choices (proxy metric, clustering, distribution-shift mitigation) than in core algorithmic advances.

Real-world OXE evaluations are conducted with a single random seed per task, and selection ratios (x%) and other hyperparameters appear tuned per task without a systematic ablation or clear guidance on how to set them, which the authors themselves acknowledge as a limitation.

Computational cost remains a concern: even the more efficient metagradient estimator costs several times more than standard training, which could limit practical adoption, especially as models/datasets scale further.

The real-world scale is still fairly modest (4 tasks, 2 embodiments), and target datasets are mostly single-task, so claims about handling large-scale multi-task curation are only partially substantiated (Droid-Multitask is the sole multi-task real-world test).

Comparisons to STRAP on LIBERO use a different evaluation protocol and policy architecture than the original paper, which, despite being explained, introduces some uncertainty about fairness of the specific numbers relative to published baselines.

No comparison to alternative policy-performance-aware baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., rollout-based scoring methods), which would help contextualize how much of the improvement stems specifically from the datamodels formulation versus simply being performance-aware.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated extension of the datamodels framework to robot imitation learning, with concrete technical solutions to challenges unique to robotics: a differentiable, rollout-free proxy metric (Eq. 5), trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce variance, and a distribution-shift mitigation strategy for heterogeneous real-world data.

Extensive empirical validation spanning 60+ tasks across three settings of increasing scale and realism: MetaWorld (50 tasks, MLP policy), LIBERO (10 tasks, transformer/diffusion Octo policy), and real-world OXE (4 tasks, 2 embodiments) — this breadth is a substantial strength relative to most data-curation papers in robotics.

Thoughtful validation that the proxy metric preserves useful signal relative to expensive rollout-based datamodels (Fig. 2, App C.1), which is a critical and non-obvious component of the method's justification.

Strong set of baselines (BR, FlowRetrieval, STRAP, AR, SR, Target-Only, All-Data/Random) and fairly rigorous, consistent evaluation protocol (fixed training steps, fixed object poses, final-checkpoint-only evaluation), improving reliability of comparisons.

Comprehensive ablations on key hyperparameters (selection %, cluster granularity, co-training ratio, extended training for All-Data baseline) that support design choices and give practitioners useful guidance.

Qualitative analyses (Figs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10) offering genuine insight into what makes DataMIL effective compared to similarity heuristics, e.g., balanced multi-source selection and correct embodiment/task retrieval even under domain shift.
Successful demonstration of cross-embodiment and multi-task data selection from OXE (Tiago-Sink, Droid-Multitask) on real hardware is a meaningful and rare achievement for this class of method.
Honest discussion of limitations, including computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and scope limited mostly to single-task target settings.
weaknesses: Real-world OXE evaluations are conducted with a single seed, and success rates are based on relatively small numbers of rollouts (e.g., 10-39 per task); this limits the statistical confidence of the headline real-world results, especially given noisy real-robot outcomes.

Concurrent work CUPID, which is closely related (uses influence functions for single-task curation), is only discussed qualitatively and not empirically compared, leaving the relative advantage of DataMIL's offline/no-rollout approach unquantified.

The metagradient-based estimator relies on a first-order Taylor approximation of a highly non-convex training process; while validated at small scale (MetaWorld pick-place-wall and a few other tasks), there is limited analysis of approximation quality/error at the scale used for LIBERO/OXE (large Octo policy, thousands of training steps), leaving the theoretical soundness at scale not fully substantiated.

Performance gains on LIBERO over the strongest heuristic baselines (Flow, STRAP) are relatively modest (37.76 vs. 35.42/34.96 average success), and several individual tasks show baselines outperforming DataMIL (e.g., Mug-Mug, Stove-Moka, Moka-Moka), somewhat tempering the 'consistent gains' claim in the abstract.

Computational cost is substantial (3-4 days on 4 A100 GPUs for OXE-scale selection) and, while framed as cheaper than real-world rollouts, this cost combined with the need for retraining/hyperparameter tuning (cluster size, selection %) may limit practical adoption, and this tradeoff is not deeply quantified against baseline retrieval methods' costs in the main text.

Discrepancy between reported LIBERO numbers and the original STRAP paper's numbers is explained post hoc (evaluation protocol and policy architecture differences) but raises some reproducibility concerns since exact comparability with prior published results is not established.

The method fundamentally requires per-task target data to compute the proxy objective, so it remains a task-specific curation approach; the single Droid-Multitask experiment is a limited test of scalability to broader multi-task/generalist curation scenarios, which is acknowledged as future work but leaves the generalist-training use case largely unaddressed.

strengths: Extends the datamodels/metagradient framework from CV/NLP to robotic imitation learning, proposing a differentiable proxy objective (BC loss on held-out target data) that avoids costly real-world rollouts during data selection.

Broad empirical scope: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 tasks, and real-world evaluation on OXE across multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid), which is more extensive than most concurrent data-curation papers in robotics.
Reasonable set of ablations (selection percentage, cluster granularity, co-training ratio, longer training for All-Data) that shed light on practical design choices.
Qualitative analysis (Figs. 5-10) offers some interesting insight into what the method selects vs. heuristic baselines, e.g. balancing multiple source datasets instead of concentrating on one.
Demonstrates selection from a genuinely unseen embodiment (Tiago) not present in the prior data, which is a meaningfully harder setting than typical similarity-based retrieval papers attempt.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited: the method largely stitches together existing techniques (Ilyas et al. datamodels, Engstrom et al. metagradient descent) with a fairly standard idea — using held-out validation/BC loss as a proxy for downstream success — which is a well-known practice in ML and not a particularly deep methodological contribution for this venue.

The critical claim that the differentiable proxy metric (validation loss) is a good stand-in for true rollout success is validated on only 1 task in the main text and 4 tasks total in the appendix, out of 50+ tasks used elsewhere; this is thin evidence for a claim that underlies the entire pipeline, especially for the LIBERO/OXE settings where only the proxy-metagradient combination is used and never checked against ground-truth rollouts at that scale.

All real-world (OXE) results are reported with a single seed and with very small evaluation counts (14-39 rollouts per task), with no variance/error bars reported in Table 1 for these settings, unlike the simulation results — this makes the real-world claims (which are a major selling point of the paper) statistically fragile.

The paper's central quantitative claim of "consistent gains" is not fully supported by Table 1: DataMIL underperforms several baselines on individual LIBERO tasks (e.g., Mug-Mug, Mug-Pudding, Stove-Moka, Bowl-Cabinet, Moka-Moka), and the aggregate improvement over the best single baseline is fairly small (37.76 vs 36.4 average) given the added complexity and compute cost of the method.

Baseline tuning appears inconsistent: STRAP is explicitly modified away from its original recommended retrieval budget (100 segments) to match DataMIL's selection percentage, which substantially changes its reported numbers (24.72% → 34.96%); this kind of post-hoc adaptation of baselines to closer performance ranges raises fairness/reproducibility concerns.
No direct empirical comparison against CUPID, the most directly related concurrent method, despite extensive discussion of it in related work — the distinction is argued only qualitatively.

The method introduces many additional hyperparameters (selection %, cluster granularity, co-training ratio, up-weighting of pre-grasp states, target-data splitting fraction for distribution-shift mitigation) that are tuned per-benchmark without a principled selection procedure, undermining the claimed practicality/generality of the approach.

Computational cost is non-trivial and sometimes prohibitive (3-4 days on 4×A100 for OXE-scale selection), which is a real barrier for the stated goal of practical, scalable data curation, yet this cost-benefit tradeoff versus simpler heuristic baselines (which are much cheaper) is not rigorously analyzed in terms of cost-normalized performance.

The Droid-Multitask success metric incorporates partial successes weighted at 0.5, an ad hoc scoring choice that is not clearly justified or shown to be applied identically and fairly across all baselines, raising some concern about potential favorable bias in reported numbers.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated adaptation of the datamodels/data-attribution framework (originally from NLP/CV) to robot imitation learning, specifically addressing the core obstacle of expensive/dangerous real-world rollouts via a differentiable proxy objective (held-out BC loss) that enables both regression-based and metagradient-based influence estimation.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation: 50 MetaWorld tasks, 10 LIBERO-10 long-horizon tasks with a large transformer/diffusion policy (Octo), and real-world experiments on heterogeneous OXE data across multiple embodiments (Franka, Tiago, Droid) and even a multi-task real-robot setting.

Thoughtful engineering contributions specific to robotics: trajectory/sub-trajectory clustering to reduce noise in influence estimates, and a practical strategy for mitigating distribution shift by mixing target data into datamodel training for real-world settings.

Strong empirical support for design choices via targeted ablations: proxy-metric vs. true-rollout correlation (Fig. 2, 11), effect of selection percentage, cluster granularity, and co-training ratio (Fig. 13), and a sanity check that simply training All-Data longer doesn't close the gap (App. C.6).

Consistent and often large improvements over multiple well-chosen baselines (SR, AR, BR, Flow, STRAP) across nearly all settings, including qualitative analyses showing DataMIL identifies task-relevant and quality-filtered data even under embodiment/domain shift (e.g., Tiago-Sink with an unseen embodiment).

Good transparency about compute cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and scope limitations in the conclusion, plus a fairly extensive and reproducible appendix (pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset construction details).
weaknesses: The core estimation machinery (regression and metagradient-based datamodels) is largely adopted from prior work (Ilyas et al. 2022; Engstrom et al. 2025) rather than newly developed here; the paper's novelty lies primarily in the proxy-metric substitution and robotics-specific engineering (clustering, distribution-shift mitigation), which are comparatively incremental.

The proxy metric's validity (correlation between held-out BC loss and true rollout success) is only rigorously validated on a handful of MetaWorld tasks (Fig. 2 and App. C.1, 4-5 tasks total) before being extended to LIBERO and OXE; it's unclear how well this correlation holds for more complex, high-dimensional visuomotor policies or truly out-of-distribution prior data.

Computational cost remains substantial (e.g., 3-4 days on 4 A100 GPUs for OXE-scale selection), which, combined with the acknowledged sensitivity to hyperparameters like selection ratio and cluster size (which appear to require per-dataset tuning without clear principled guidance), somewhat limits practical plug-and-play applicability.
Real-world OXE evaluations are conducted with a single seed, limiting the statistical confidence of the real-robot results despite the otherwise appealing scale of experimentation.

Concurrent related work CUPID is discussed only qualitatively (no direct empirical comparison), and it is unclear how DataMIL's offline approach would fare against CUPID's online policy-gradient influence estimation in matched settings.

In LIBERO task-wise results (Table 1), DataMIL's advantage over the strongest heuristic baselines (STRAP, BR, Flow) is often modest or occasionally reversed on individual tasks, suggesting the average improvement is somewhat driven by consistency rather than uniformly dominant performance.
